title: The Sheep Who Counted Children
blurb: A sheep gets the job backwards — and it works.

lesson.ask: Tilly tried one way, then another way. What is something you tried twice today?
lesson.fact: Real sheep really do sleep about four hours a night — but they nap a lot, all day long.

body: It was nearly bedtime in the green field at the top of the hill. The sun had gone soft and orange. The birds had stopped shouting and started whispering.
In the middle of that field stood one small sheep. Her name was Tilly. Tilly had one job, and everyone knew what it was.

"Count the children," said the old sheep. "That is what we do. A child lies in bed. You count. One child. Two children. Three children. And by the time you reach the sleepy ones, the child in the bed is fast asleep."
Tilly nodded. "Count the children. I can do that."
That night, Tilly stood by the fence and got ready. She took a deep breath. She looked at the sleeping houses. And then she counted.
"One CHILD," said Tilly, very loudly.
Nothing happened.
"Two CHILDREN," said Tilly, even more loudly.
Nothing happened. In a house at the bottom of the hill, a little girl sat up in bed and said, "Mum? I think there is a sheep shouting."
Tilly tried again. "THREE CHILDREN! FOUR CHILDREN! FIVE CHILDREN!"
Windows went on. Doors opened. A man in his pyjamas came outside and said, "Is everybody all right? Who is shouting numbers?"
"Me," said Tilly. "I am counting the children. It is my job. It is meant to make them sleepy."
The man in pyjamas looked at Tilly for a long moment. Then he said, "Have you tried counting something quieter?"
Tilly thought about this. She looked at the field. She looked at the sky. And then she saw them — small, soft, and moving very slowly across the dark: clouds.
"One cloud," said Tilly, quietly. "Two clouds. Three clouds."
In the house at the bottom of the hill, the little girl lay back down. The shouting had stopped. There was just a soft voice outside, going slowly past three, past four, past five.
"Six clouds," said Tilly. "Seven. Eight."
The little girl's eyes got heavy. "Nine clouds," said Tilly, and yawned. "Ten."
By eleven she had forgotten what she was counting. By twelve she was asleep with her chin on the fence, and the whole hill was quiet.
The old sheep found her there in the morning. "Did you count the children?" she asked.
"No," said Tilly. "I counted clouds. But everyone went to sleep anyway."
The old sheep thought about it for a while. Then she nodded. "Well," she said. "That is the same thing, only nicer."

And after that, every night, in that field, you could hear a small sheep going quietly through the sky: one cloud, two clouds, three — until the whole hill, sheep and children both, fell asleep together.
THE END.

title: Marvin and the Very Serious Puddle
blurb: A puddle has a very important job. Marvin has boots.

lesson.ask: The puddle was holding the sky. What is something that looks small but is actually doing a big job?
lesson.fact: A puddle holds the whole sky, upside down — every puddle is a mirror lying flat on the ground.

body: After the rain, the whole pavement was covered in puddles. Small ones. Medium ones. And one enormous one, right outside Marvin's gate, shaped like Australia.
Marvin put on his boots. Marvin's boots were yellow, and they made a sound that Marvin liked very much: squelch.
"Marvin," said his mother. "If you jump in that puddle, you will be wet from your hat to your socks."
Marvin looked at the puddle. The puddle looked back, very calmly, the way a puddle does.
"I understand," said Marvin.
He was not lying. He understood completely. He understood that the puddle was enormous, that his boots were yellow, and that some things in life are simply meant to be jumped in.
So he jumped.
SPLASH.
It was a magnificent splash. It went up. It went sideways. It went into the hedge, where a blackbird was sitting, minding its own business. The blackbird made a noise like a rusty door and flew away.
Marvin stood in the middle of the puddle, wet from his hat to his socks, feeling extremely good.
And then the puddle spoke.
"Excuse me," said the puddle.
Marvin froze.
"I said excuse me," said the puddle. "I am working."
"Working?" said Marvin.

"Working," said the puddle. "I am an enormous puddle. Do you know how much sky I have to hold? I am holding the entire sky, upside down, all day. Clouds. Birds. One aeroplane, twice. It is a very big job and I am doing it very well, and then somebody in yellow boots comes along and jumps straight through the middle of my sky."
Marvin looked down. He could see the sky in the puddle, in pieces now, wobbling.
"I'm sorry," he said. "I didn't know you were busy."
"Nobody ever does," said the puddle, rather sadly. "Puddles look like nothing. That is exactly why we get jumped on."
Marvin stood still in the water and thought about being looked at and thought to be nothing. He did not like the way it felt.
"Can I help?" he said.
The puddle went quiet for a moment. "Well," it said. "You could stop standing in the middle of me."
Marvin stepped out, carefully, and stood on the dry bit by the gate.
Slowly, very slowly, the puddle got its sky back. A cloud came in. Then a whole tree, upside down. Then the sun, which was pleased to be included.
"Better," said the puddle. "Much better. Thank you."
And Marvin found that he was wet, and cold, and had a hole in one sock, and he did not mind one bit. He had made friends with a puddle, which is not a thing most people manage before breakfast.

The next morning, the puddle had gone somewhere to do its next job. But it had left something behind: a perfectly round, flat, dry circle of pavement, exactly the size of a puddle, and right in the middle of it, one small feather — the blackbird's, from the day before.
Marvin kept it in a tin.
And he never jumped in an enormous puddle again, unless he had first asked politely.
THE END.

title: The Loudest Sock in the World
blurb: A new sock arrives. The sock has opinions.

lesson.ask: The sock could not be quiet. How did {{name}} help it?
lesson.fact: Your feet have about a quarter of all the bones in your body — 52 of them, and your toes do half the work of balancing.

body: On Monday, {{namePos}} opened the drawer and found a new sock. It was red, with one green stripe, and the moment the drawer opened, the sock said:
"HELLO!"
{{name}} jumped.
"I AM THE LOUDEST SOCK IN THE WORLD," said the sock, happily. "AND I HAVE BEEN IN THIS DRAWER FOR SIX DAYS."
"Socks can't talk," said {{name}}.
"WRONG," said the sock. "Socks can't talk QUIETLY. That is different, and it is my whole problem."
So {{name}} put the sock on. It was warm. It was comfortable. It also shouted comments about everything it saw.
"WHAT A BIG KITCHEN," said the sock. "IS THAT THE KETTLE? I LIKE IT. I LIKE EVERYTHING HERE."
At breakfast, {{name}} put the sock's foot under the table. "Please," whispered {{name}}. "Please be quieter. People are looking."
"OKAY," said the sock. Then, a second later: "THE TOAST IS VERY GOOD."

At school, things got worse. During quiet reading, the sock said, "I CANNOT SEE THE PICTURES FROM DOWN HERE." During maths, the sock said, "NINE LOOKS LIKE A BALLOON." During the bit where everyone had to be completely silent, the sock said, in its biggest voice: "THIS IS MY FAVOURITE PART!"
Twenty-three children turned to look at {{name}}'s foot.
After school, {{name}} sat on the front step and had a serious talk with the sock.
"You are getting me in trouble," said {{name}}. "You have to learn to be quiet, or you have to live in the drawer."
The sock was quiet for a long time. So long that {{name}} thought it had gone. Then it said, in a small voice:
"I don't know how."
{{name}} thought about this. It is hard to know how to do something nobody has shown you.
"Right," said {{name}}. "We'll practise. When I press your toe, that means quiet. When I squeeze your heel, that means you can talk."
"And nothing else?" said the sock.
"Nothing else," said {{name}}.
They practised all evening. Press the toe — quiet. Squeeze the heel — "HELLO." Press the toe — quiet.
By bedtime, the sock could do it.
That night {{name}} wore the sock to bed, which was unusual, but the sock was warm and had had a hard week.
"Squeeze or press?" whispered the sock.
"Squeeze," said {{name}}.
The sock thought for a moment. Then it said, as quietly as it could — which for the loudest sock in the world was still not very quiet, but it was trying:
"Goodnight. I like you. I like everything here."
And {{name}} fell asleep, warm, with one green stripe showing above the covers.
THE END.

title: The Boat With No Light
blurb: The lantern goes out. The little boat finds the bank by ear.

lesson.ask: When it is dark at home, what sound tells you that everything is all right?
lesson.fact: The moon makes no light of its own. Everything you see up there is sunlight bounced off grey dust, and it has to travel 384,400 kilometres to reach your eyes, which takes about a second and a quarter.

body: It was the last crossing of the day. The river had gone flat and smooth, and the sky was going from orange to blue.
Along the bank the lamps came on one at a time. click, click, click, as if somebody were turning them on.
Mr Ash waited in his boat with his oars. He had been in it for thirty-one years and had an opinion about most things. The only other passenger was Nell.
"Can I carry the lantern?" said Nell.
"It wants to stay in the boat," said Mr Ash. "Out on the bow it would fill with water, and I'd find my way home by ear."
So it hung in the middle, making a small yellow circle on the water. Mr Ash pushed off.
Halfway across, the wind got up in one soft push, and pfft, the lantern went out. It made no sound at all.
But it was the same boat, and the oars went plip, plip, plip.
"That's only the wind," said Mr Ash. "It's a friendly wind. Four minutes to the steps."
The far wall had a lamp on top, and it was how she knew which steps were hers. Now there was only dark, and dark is full of shapes that are all more or less the right shape.
Mr Ash stopped rowing, and the boat drifted on until it stopped too.
"Two sets of steps on that side," he said. "The big ones, and the little ones by the boathouse. With a light they look different. Without, they don't."
"I know this river like the back of my hand," said Mr Ash. "The hand isn't helping tonight."
"Can we listen?" said Nell. Mr Ash said nothing, which from Mr Ash was a great deal.
Nell put her head on one side. The water was soft on one side, and on the other it went over stones: hiss, hiss, hiss, like a finger along a comb.
"That's the bank," said Nell. "It's the stones by our steps. The steps make a different noise, and then it goes deep by the wall."
Nell nodded, in the dark, where nobody could see it. "I know that sound the way you know the stairs at home."
Mr Ash put the oars back in and rowed towards where she was listening. He never said she was right. He was not that sort of man.
The hissing came nearer, up over the side of the boat, and the wood knocked against something solid. click.
"Steps on the left," said Mr Ash. "You're quite right, Nell — sit down, I have to tie up, and that takes two hands."

He lit the lantern on the top step, and its yellow square lay on the water, and the water was pleased with it. They walked up together, the lantern swinging between them, and the river went back to being a big dark nothing.

At Nell's gate there was a cup of milk on the table, and the window upstairs was showing the moon. Nell thought about all that light coming such a long way to reach her face. Then she went to bed, and the story came down after her.
THE END.

title: The Book That Was Left Out
blurb: One book stays out after closing time. Nobody came back for it.

lesson.ask: If somebody drew a picture of your bedroom, what would you want them to draw?
lesson.fact: The little pocket in the back of a library book, holding a card with the day it must be returned, was invented in 1905 at Newark Public Library. Almost every library in the world has copied it since.

body: At closing time the lamps went off one at a time down the long table, until only the low green one on the desk was burning.
Miss Hall walked the last round with the trolley, and Biscuit the cat rode on top, because that was the best place.
Ada came too, because checking the tables was her job, and Ada did it very slowly, so as not to finish it.
On table seven was a book that wasn't on the trolley, lying face up, as though somebody had been called away.
"Somebody left that out," said Miss Hall. "It will find its shelf in the morning, and whoever borrowed it can have a polite letter."
Ada picked it up. It was heavy, and bigger than a book with stories in it, and the cloth was grey, and the spine said nothing.
In the back cover was a pocket with a card in it, a day written in blue pencil. "That's a long time ago," said Ada, reading it upside down.
"It will be in here somewhere, then," said Miss Hall, who had not looked. "Put it in the box. Biscuit, get down."
The book wouldn't go into the box. Ada tried twice, and in the end it lay on the trolley like a heavy whale.
So Ada opened it, and it fell open in the middle all by itself. A photograph slid out, face up.
It was a photograph of the reading room.
Ada didn't understand at first, because it looked exactly like the place she was standing: the tall windows, the long table, the low green lamp.
And there, on the middle of the carpet, a small girl in a coat sat holding a big grey book with nothing on the spine.
Ada looked at the book in her hands, and then at the picture, and then at the picture again.
"That's the same book," said Miss Hall. She looked at the picture for some time. "Well," she said. "It has been round."
"But it's in the picture of this room," said Ada. "With her in it, holding it. So it was on this carpet, and now it's here."
"Books do that," said Miss Hall. "That is the whole job of a book. It goes off somewhere and waits, and then it comes back."
They did not put it in the box. Miss Hall set it on the middle table, in the pool of the lamp, and laid the photograph back.
Then the big lights went off, all but the one on the desk, and the trolley went squeak, squeak, squeak. After that there were no sounds at all in the building.
Ada's mother came up the path with her coat open, and Ada told her about the small girl on the carpet the whole way home, twice.
And in the library, in the dark, the big grey book lay open at the photograph, with the little girl in the coat holding it. The room had come back into the book, and the book stayed in the room.
Ada was asleep before her mother had finished the second telling, and the lamp stayed on a little longer than it needed to.
THE END.

title: The Shell That Was Not Broken
blurb: A shell with a crack down it. Somebody small is moving inside.

lesson.ask: Is there something you were a bit scared of that turned out to be something else?
lesson.fact: A hermit crab has no shell of its own. It borrows an empty snail shell, and when it has grown too big for it, it has to go and find a bigger one, so it always tries the hole that fits.

body: The sea had gone out a long way that evening, so far that the water was a grey line along the edge of the sky.
The sky was pink at the top and orange underneath, and the pools in the sand were holding all of it.
Tam and Grandad walked the wet sand, looking for what the tide had brought in. The sea loses things and never once says sorry.
Tam picked things up and put them down again. Grandad carried a bag and said nothing, which kept the evening going.
Then Tam found a big one.
It was a shell the size of two hands, white going pink at the tip, with a long crack down the side and a piece gone from the lip.
Tam did not pick it up at once. Then, with two hands, very slowly, the way you pick up something that is asleep.
"We're taking this home," said Tam.
"Tam," Grandad said, without raising his voice. "Put it back down. Nothing lives in a broken shell."
"They want the good ones," said Grandad. "They need the good ones. That is the whole of it."
Tam did not put it down, and did not argue either. Tam just held it, and looked at the crack, and thought.
And then Tam heard something.
tap. tap.
It was not the sea, which was a long grey line away. It came from inside the shell, and it was very small, and very polite.
Tam knelt down in the wet sand, put the shell down gently, crack facing up, and waited.
Grandad started to say something, and Tam put one finger up, and Grandad stopped.
Nothing much happened for quite a while. Then the crack widened, and out came one claw, purple, with a cream stripe, testing the air.
Then the other one. Then a face, all eyes. And a soft pale body, not at all like a crab out of a picture.
And the crab turned round and backed into the shell and made itself at home, and the crack stayed exactly as it had come out.
It wasn't a broken shell. It was a door.
"Oh," said Grandad. "Oh, I see. I have been wrong about shells for a long time." He sat down beside Tam in the wet sand, which took a while.
Tam waited until the crab had stopped moving before standing up, because Tam had learned that things need a minute.
And further down the sand there were more shells: dozens of them, all on their sides, all with the same long crack. Some were moving.
It was nearly dark. They walked back up the beach with the shells still where they were, and the sea came in behind them, taking its time.
Grandad carried the bag home and never complained. At the door he said, "Next time you find one, you can have a proper look. Just don't be too keen."
Tam thought about that on the stairs. A thing can look completely finished and still have somebody living in it.
Then Tam was in bed with the window pushed up a bit, and the sea going on out there in the dark. The sound came, and went, and came again.
THE END.

title: The Music Box in the Attic
blurb: Everything in the attic is finished. One small thing still plays.

lesson.ask: Is there something in your house that everybody says is finished, but it still works?
lesson.fact: Inside a music box there is a little drum covered in tiny pins. When you wind it, the drum turns slowly underneath a metal comb, and every pin flicks one tooth and makes exactly one note.

body: The attic smelled of boxes and old paper, and it was still warm up under the roof.
{{name}} and Grandad went up at half past six with one torch. The ladder creaked, the hatch banged, and they stood in the blue evening.
There was a great deal up there: boxes, a bicycle, a chair with one arm, a lamp with no bulb, and a clock that had stopped.
They were after the blue box: the good lamp, the candles, and the jumper Grandad had once been far taller than. It was under the bicycle, which did not move, and neither did Grandad.
Then Grandad said, "Right. The box. And no, nothing up here works. Everything up here's finished. Nothing in this attic works any more."
{{name}} put a hand out to point at the blue box, then took it back, because {{namePos}} own idea was to listen. Not to Grandad. To the attic.
And something was ticking on the floor, very small and out of step with itself, and coming from the smallest box, the one with a horse on the lid.
Grandad said, "That is nothing. It is the house settling. It does that."
But the noise was not above {{name}}. It was below, and ticking things do not go on and off like that, and they both got down to look.
Inside was a small wooden box the colour of tea, with a horse on the lid and a metal handle.
Grandad said, "Leave that. It has not played since before your mother was born. There is no spring in it."
But {{name}} turned the handle. Nothing happened. {{name}} turned it again, and nothing happened at all.
Grandad said, "There. Finished." And he sat down on an old suitcase, the way you do when you have said what you came to say.
{{name}} turned the handle a third time, all the way round, until it came back to where it started.
And the little drum inside began to turn. tick rattle, tick rattle, and a sound came out that neither of them had heard for years.
It was a tune: a small thin one with a wobble in the middle, getting slower, and slower, and the last notes hung in the air.
Grandad did not say anything. He sat on the suitcase with the torch up at the roof, and listened to it all.
"Well," he said. "It doesn't need a spring." "No," said {{name}}. "It just needed turning."
And then it needed turning again, so {{name}} turned it, and it played the same tune, and the window went blue to black.
They found the blue box in about a minute, with the jumper inside it, exactly where Grandad had said.
And at the bottom of the stairs the little box sat playing with the lid open, and the tune went down the corridor and up the stairs after them.
It was still going when {{name}} was upstairs, and slower, and slower. Then it stopped in the middle of a bar, the way a song does.
Grandad carried it back up in the dark, and the hatch shut with a sound like a lid. In the morning the house was full of that same ticking.
THE END.

title: The Kettle That Would Not Go Quiet
blurb: The kitchen will not stop clicking. Nobody can say why.

lesson.ask: Which sound in your house would you still like to hear when everything else has gone quiet?
lesson.fact: A kettle whistles when tiny swirls of steam come off the water and beat against the inside of the spout. Cambridge engineers only worked that out in 2013, more than a hundred years after people had started asking.

body: The house was asleep, and the kitchen was not.
It was just past midnight. The oven light was on, and the window over the sink was black and shiny as a plate.
Dad was asleep in the chair by the table, with a cup of tea he had made before his shift. The tea had gone completely cold.
And the kettle on the hob would not stop.
Click, click, click. Off, then on. Then off, click, click, click, like a very small clock that had lost its way.
Wren came down in her socks, which she was not supposed to do, and stood in the doorway to listen.
"Dad," she said. "The kettle is clicking."
Dad opened one eye. "Switch it off at the plug, love. That'll do it."
Wren pulled the plug out. The flex hung down like a tired arm.
Click. Click. Click.
The kettle carried on regardless.
"Fault in the wiring," said Dad, putting his head back against the chair. "We'll ring the shop in the morning."
Wren stayed where she was. The little light on the kettle was still on, and in that dark kitchen it was the size of a full moon.
She walked over and looked at it for a long time.
"Dad," she said. "Has it got any water in it?"
Dad sat up. The chair complained about it. He lifted the lid and put his face right down over the inside of the kettle, which is what you have to do to see.
"Oh," said Dad.
The kettle was bone dry. He had boiled the last of the water before his shift and then put it back to remind himself to switch it off, and it had been trying to boil nothing ever since.
"Well," said Dad, in a voice that was working quite hard. "That is my fault."
Wren went to the cold tap and filled the kettle right to the top. The water was very loud in the quiet kitchen. It made her jump, and then she liked it.
She set it back down, pressed the button, and stood well back.
Click. The kettle woke up. A low hum, and a rattle underneath it, and then the whistle, going up and up like something climbing out of a hole.
Then, all on its own, it stopped.
Dad sat down again. "Well," he said. "It was thirsty."
And since the water was hot, and it was half past midnight, they made two mugs of hot chocolate in the good cups and sat in the dark kitchen and listened to the fridge humming underneath everything.
"Why does it go higher when the water's nearly gone?" Wren asked.
"Little swirls," said Dad. "Big lazy ones first. Then smaller, and faster, and faster, until they sound like somebody screaming."
Wren put her ear close to the kettle. It was cooling now: tick, tick, tick, slower, and slower, and quieter, a thing that had finished working, resting.
They carried the cups up the stairs in both hands, slowly, and nobody said anything, because there was nothing left to say and it was very late.
And from the top of the stairs you could still hear the kettle going tick, tick, tick, like a small heart remembering how to be slower.
THE END.

title: Mr. Barrow's Last Round
blurb: One thing left in the bag, and the last house has no number.

lesson.ask: If you could send one small thing to somebody far away, what would you put in the envelope?
lesson.fact: The first postage stamp in the world was the Penny Black, in 1840. It had no country written on it at all, because in those days there was only one country posting letters.

body: At five past eight the lamps were on all along Mill Row, and Mr. Barrow was out on his round.
He was the last postman to go that day. The big letters were done and the big bags were back on the van. Only the small bag was left, with one single thing in it.
It was not a letter.
It was flat, and brown, and very light. Lighter than a birthday card, almost. There was a stamp in one corner and an address in pencil across the front.
"That is a strange thing," said Mr. Barrow, to nobody at all. He said it quite seriously, the way you do about a job.
He got back on his bicycle and rode the last of the round slowly, because it was nearly time to go home. The last house on the whole round was number 41, and it was in his book.
He could not find number 41.
Not because it wasn't there. It was right at the end of the row, behind a gate and a hedge, with one light on in the kitchen.
But somebody had painted the front of the house a new colour, and the new colour was exactly the colour the number used to be.
So all that was left was a house. Number 41 had gone. Mr. Barrow looked at his book, and then at the hedge, and then at the book again.
He was just turning back for the depot when a voice came out from behind the gate.
"Are you looking for me?"
A small child in a dressing gown stood in the gap, holding the gate shut with one knee.
Mr. Barrow took off his hat. He felt strongly that this was the correct thing to do.
"Are you number 41?" he asked.
"No," said the child. "We're on the corner. The number's under the paint, and you can only see it in the rain."
"Then I believe this is yours," said Mr. Barrow, and held out the little brown thing.
The child did not take it. They looked at it for a long moment. "That's mine," they said. "I posted it this morning."
Mr. Barrow looked at the address, which was in very small writing, and belonged to the house they were both standing in front of.
"You posted it to yourself."
"Yes," said the child, and nodded, as if this were a perfectly ordinary thing that everybody did every day.
It was not a thing that everybody did every day. It was the very first letter the child had ever sent, of any kind, ever.
Mr. Barrow asked for a name and wrote it in his book, and asked them to sign for it, and the child signed very slowly with a long squiggle.
"I've never had a letter before," said the child. "I wanted to see if they really come."
And they had come. That was the whole surprise of the evening.
The postman had no more deliveries, so he sat down on the low wall by the gate, the child sat down beside him, and together they read the letter out loud under the street lamp.
It was not very long. It said: Dear me. I hope you are still nine, and that you still like the sea. I did it.
Mr. Barrow said it was a very good letter, and that he had delivered a great many worse ones.
Then he got back on his bicycle, said goodnight, and rode the half mile to the depot whistling, with an empty bag that felt about as light as the letter had been.
And the child stood in the doorway until his little red light went round the corner and was gone, and then went inside, and put the letter on the table, and read it again.
THE END.

title: The Bike That Would Not Go Slow
blurb: One small problem with a good bike: going slowly.

lesson.ask: What is something at home you could do more slowly and it would still work perfectly well?
lesson.fact: The back wheel of a bicycle has a freewheel on it, a little ratchet that lets the wheel keep turning after your feet have stopped, which is why a bike coasts downhill all on its own.

body: The bicycle had belonged to Grandad, and now it belonged to {{name}}, which is a thing that happens to a great many bicycles.
It was a good bike. It was dark green, with a bell on the handlebars and a basket on the front and one slow squeak out of the back wheel.
{{namePos}} first proper ride was down the long hill on the green, which was the best part and the worst part.

The top of the hill was quiet. There were nettles at the top, and a gate, and a view of the whole town with all its little lights on. At the bottom there was a wall, a bench, and about nine metres of grass.
Grandad walked beside and held on to the back of the saddle. It was lovely. It was the loveliest thing that had ever happened to anybody.
And then the hill started to go.
A bicycle with nobody on the pedals is only a heavy thing on a slope, and this one let go like it had been waiting all afternoon to.
{{name}} did not scream. That part comes afterwards. {{name}} simply held on very hard to the handlebars and watched the grass come up to meet the front wheel.
It arrived.
The bike stopped, and the basket came off. Nothing was broken, and {{namePos}} heart was going, and Grandad said, quite calmly, "Right. Now the brakes."
"Both of them?" said {{name}}.
"Both at once," said Grandad. "Squeeze the two together. That is the trick, that is."
So {{name}} squeezed the two brakes together.
SHREEK.
It was the loudest noise the green had ever heard. The front wheel wobbled, and {{name}} put both feet down into the grass and stopped the whole thing with {{namePos}} own knees.
{{name}} sat there afterwards breathing very hard, while a blackbird explained what it thought about the entire business.
Grandad nodded slowly.
"Well," he said. "You are one who stops with both brakes."
And {{name}} was not one who stopped with both brakes. That was not quite the right answer, and {{name}} did not know it yet.
The trouble was that {{name}} wanted to go down that hill again, which was perfectly reasonable and also the end of everything.
"Go on, then," said Grandad. "I'll walk down beside you."
But halfway down, something in {{name}} thought: what happens if I stop pedalling?
{{name}} took both feet off the pedals and held them up in the air.
The bike went on by itself. Slowly.

The air pushed back a little. The hill gave a little back. The basket stayed on. The whole thing came down the green as gently as a leaf on a pond, while {{namePos}} legs did absolutely nothing at all.
At the bottom, {{name}} put one foot on the path.
And it stopped.
"There," said Grandad. "It had it in it the whole time: a freewheel, which lets the back wheel carry on turning once your feet stop. It was never the brakes. It was only ever speed."
{{name}} went back up the hill and did it eleven more times, which took most of the evening, and every single one of them was a little slower than the one before.
By the time the sky had gone properly dark, going slowly had stopped feeling like something {{name}} had to work at, and had started to feel like the best part of the whole day.
Grandad unhooked the basket and hung it on his own handlebars, and they walked home, and the one slow squeak out of the back wheel went tick, tick, tick, all the way down the lane.
THE END.

title: The Worm Under the Garden Slab
blurb: The long way round to the warm heap. The short way is under the path.

lesson.ask: What do you like to do while you are waiting for a slow thing to happen?
lesson.fact: An earthworm has no eyes at all and does not need them. It has light-sensitive cells in its skin instead, so it knows when it is out in the open and can head back down.

body: Under the garden path it is always evening.
There is no light down there and no wind, and the earth is warm after a whole sunny day in it.
Mabel lay in the warm earth and moved her back a little, to see how it felt.
It felt excellent.
Past the fence and past the bean sticks was the compost heap, and the heap was where Mabel went when she wanted to be warm for a long time.
Tonight, Mabel wanted to be warm for a long time.
So she set off down her tunnel, which she knew well, because it was her tunnel.
She went past the roots of the beans, which tickled. She went past the flat grey stone that tasted of nothing, which was her favourite one.
And then she came to the slab.
It was a long grey thing that went right across her tunnel, and it was not going anywhere.
Mabel pushed it. She pushed it for a very long time, with her front end, and then with her back, which is the proper way to push.
The slab stayed exactly where it was.
So Uncle Tub came along. Uncle Tub was a mole, and Uncle Tub was very pleased about all of it.
"Going under, are you," said Uncle Tub. "Good, that is the way. Feel along it with your nose and keep on going. I have never been stopped by a slab."
So Mabel felt along it with her nose, and kept on going.
She went under a great deal of path, and past a fence post, and past a root the size of her arm. It was dark, and it was still going. It was a slab the whole way.
Mabel stopped. And she lay there in the dark, quite cross, and listened, which she had not bothered to do before.
Above her, the feet of children went past. Patter, patter. Their boots were saying things she could not hear.
Then she heard something else. Not above. Off to the left.
It was a sound like sugar being poured very slowly, and Mabel knew that sound well, because it was an old road.
Ants had made it, and beetles had made it, and the little white roots of a birch tree had woven through it and packed it soft.
So Mabel turned left. Down a bit, and round, and up a bit, and round again. It was the long way, and the wrong way, and the way that takes all night.
She went along it anyway, because the earth on the left was soft, and the earth on the right was hard.
By the time she was warm and tired, the beans were overhead, and then the sky, with a few stars in it, and a smell of old apples.
And then the earth opened.
Not much. Only at the end of her nose. Only enough to get her head out and have a look around.
Mabel was at the bottom of the compost heap, at the warm end, in the dark.
It was warm, and it smelled of everything that had ever been in that garden. Mabel lay back down into it until there was nothing of her left to look at.
Above her, the garden went to bed. The little lights went out in the houses, one by one.
The path stayed where it was. Nobody knew that under the middle of it there was a new tunnel, and there would still be one there in the morning.
Mabel did not have to hurry. That was the good part. She had the whole warm night, and she was right in the middle of it.
THE END.

title: The Sweater with One Long Sleeve
blurb: One sleeve is much too long. It takes a whole night to see why.

lesson.ask: Somebody in your house has made something just for you. Do you know what it is for?
lesson.fact: Real knitters count on purpose. Lots of knitting patterns tell you to make one sleeve longer, so your hands can slip inside it and stay warm.

body: It was a cold Friday at the little house at the end of the lane. By eight o'clock the sky had gone the colour of a plum.
There was a parcel on the table with string round it, and it had been there since the morning. {{name}} had spent all day trying not to look at it.
It was from Nan. {{name}} knew that because of the string, which Nan always tied in the same way.
At the door Nan had said one thing. "One of them is longer. I counted on purpose. Leave it alone."
Inside the parcel was a soft green sweater with two rows of small buttons. {{name}} put it on straight away, and {{namePos}} fingers went warm at once.
Then {{name}} looked down at the two sleeves. One came down to the wrist, like a sleeve should.
The other one was much, much longer. It came past the knuckles and right down over the hand.
"That one is broken," said {{name}}.
So {{name}} pulled the long sleeve up so that the two of them would match. It slid straight back down, with a soft whoosh.
So {{name}} tried it rolled up instead. Rolled up, it was a fat lump, and it came loose while the tea was brewing.
The cuff button shot off and went under the table. It was a quarter past six before {{name}} found it.
An hour went past, and the sweater was no better.
After that {{name}} sat down and looked at the sweater for a very long time.
The green wool had a small hole in it, and one loose thread, and the hem was a bit crooked, and it was still the best thing in the room.
Then {{name}} put the sweater over the back of the chair, and left it sitting in the dark with its sleeves hanging down.
At bedtime the room went cold. It did that every night.
The cold came up through the floor first, and then sat at the end of the bed like a cat that would not be told.
{{name}} got out of bed and picked the sweater up. Both hands went round the long sleeve.
"I did it on purpose," said {{name}} out loud, just to hear how it sounded.
Then {{name}} put the sweater on, and slid {{namePos}} right hand up inside the long sleeve, the way you slide a hand into a pocket.
And it was warm. Not hot. Warm the way a cup is warm.
The cold came off {{namePos}} hand and went away down the wool, all the way past the elbow.
{{name}} stood there in the dark room with one hand in and one hand out, and said absolutely nothing at all.
Nan had not knitted a broken sleeve and got the arms to match. Nan had knitted a pocket.
The cold comes at night, and now the cold had somewhere to put {{namePos}} hand.
Nothing in the house was broken, {{name}} decided, climbing back into bed.
It was only that a thing made for the night is a very hard thing to see in the daytime.
The long sleeve went along the pillow beside {{namePos}} face, warm as a paw. Outside, the wind went past the window and on.
{{namePos}} hand stayed warm, and the wool had a hole in it, and a loose thread, and it was not broken at all.
Goodnight, sweater.
THE END.

title: The Night the Sky Filled Up
blurb: A cat counts the sky. Three stars, one owl, and a long wait.

lesson.ask: Is there a window in your house where you can see the sky from your bed?
lesson.fact: It takes about twenty to thirty minutes for your eyes to get used to the dark. After that, stars that were there the whole time come out.

body: It was the middle of the night, and the house was asleep, and the moon was not out. The moon takes the night off now and then.
On this night it had things to do elsewhere. In the garden there was a shed, and on the shed there was a small grey cat called Nell, and Nell was not asleep.
She was looking at the sky. That was the whole of her plan, and there was nothing else in the garden worth looking at, except the sky, and tonight it had almost nothing in it.
One star. Two. Three.
The three of them sat up in the cold, not saying anything, and the rest of the sky was dark all the way down to the trees.
"That is not a sky," said Nell. "That is a sky with the rest taken off."
So she counted them properly, the way you count sheep, or steps, or anything else you need to get through. One, two, three, four.
Then she could not find the fifth. She looked to the left and the sky was empty, and she looked to the right and the sky was empty.
"They are going out," said Nell. "Every time I look, there is one fewer."
The stars held absolutely still.
She tried harder. She made her eyes into little holes, the way cats do when they are being extremely serious, and she counted again. One, two, three, exactly as before.
Not one more, and not one less either, which was a small comfort. On the gatepost there was an old owl, who had heard all of it.
"You are looking too hard," said the owl. "I count them. It is a full-time job, and it takes all night, and I have been doing it for a very long time."
"How many are there?" said Nell. The owl did not answer. That was a question about her job.
Nell wanted to know very much. So she sat on the shed roof and kept looking, and the sky stayed nearly empty.
Her eyes began to hurt a little. The wind came over the field and went through her fur and put it up in the wrong places.
At some point, without deciding to, she shut her eyes.
And behind her shut eyes there was the sound of the house going on without her. The fridge humming, the clock doing tick, and a long way off a dog who was also awake.
And while she was not looking, the sky got on with it. Stars came out behind the ridge, and then more stars, further along, quietly, in ones and twos.
It was the way lights come on in a street after everyone has gone to bed. It took a long time, and that is the good part.
Nell opened one eye, because she was a cat, and a cat cannot help it.
The sky was full.
The moon was out after all, sitting low and pale with a whole cold lake of her own light, and there were so many stars that Nell could not count them.
The four were all still there. And the fifth she had lost somewhere in the middle.
"The stars are very rude," said Nell. "They make you wait."
She had looked at the sky all night to find out what it was doing, and she had also spent all night letting the sky get on with it.
Then she stood up on the shed roof and stretched, and looked once more, and the sky was still full.
And it was turning, very slowly, the way it has turned since before anybody was alive, one star at a time, all the way round the pole star, which is the one that does not move.
There was no hurry about any of it. Nell came down off the shed and went to find somewhere warmer, and the garden went back to being a garden.
The light stayed exactly where it was, and so did the dark, and so did the house, ticking, with the garden in the middle of it and the sky on top.
And one small grey cat went slowly to sleep in between.
THE END.
